title: The one whose aim succeeds
hookLine: the naming; the brahmins read the marks: a great king or a great teacher
last: SEVEN DAYS — LOVE CAN BE ADOPTED.

cards: Somebody chose your name. Maybe after a grandparent, maybe from a book, maybe because it sounded good with your last name. Every name carries a little wish.
Today the baby in the palace gets his. The king invites a hundred and eight brahmins to a feast, the story says, to name the child and to tell his future. Eight of them are the wisest.

teach.b: They name him Siddhattha, in Pali, or Siddhartha, the Sanskrit form more familiar in English. Siddha means accomplished, succeeded. Attha means aim, goal, purpose.
So: the one whose aim succeeds. Gotama is the family name, and the Sakyas are his people, which is why he's later called Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas. Then the eight brahmins read his body.
Buddhist texts describe thirty-two marks of a great man, signs a trained eye was said to recognize.
In the later tellings, seven of them raise two fingers: two possibilities. If he stays home, he'll be a king who rules the whole world. If he leaves home, he'll be a buddha.
The same prophecy his parents heard after the dream.
But the youngest of the eight, Kondañña, raises one finger. He says there's only one road for this child: he will leave, and become a buddha.
Hold on to that name; Kondañña comes back much later, at a very important moment. Now stand where the king stands. One road leads to an empire, his son on the throne, the family's future secure.
The other leads out the palace gate, and away. You can guess which a father would hope for, and that hope will shape everything the king does for years.
For now, the baby just has a name: a wish, and, the story says, a promise.

how: Buddhists know the Buddha as Siddhattha Gotama, or Siddhartha Gautama, and as Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas; the naming and the reading of the marks are told in temple art and in stories for children.

o: his clan name, shared with all the Sakyas
his given name: the one whose aim succeeds
a title meaning the one who woke up fully

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.

s: Siddhartha means 'the one whose aim succeeds'
all the brahmins agreed he would become a buddha
seven said king or buddha; only the youngest, Kondañña, said buddha alone.
Siddhattha Gotama, of the Sakya people.

games.q: you're Kondañña, the youngest brahmin. seven older, wiser men have raised two fingers: king or buddha. what do you do?
o: raise two fingers too. they're older.
raise one finger: he will become a buddha.
games.why: he raises one finger. only one road for this child. and Kondañña will return, much later, at a very important moment.

practice: Say your own full name slowly, out loud or silently, as if you'd never heard it before. Who chose it, and what might they have hoped for you?
Hear the wish without needing to agree with it, then let your name go quiet and rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Siddhattha. Siddhartha in Sanskrit: the one whose aim succeeds. The Buddha's given name, chosen at a feast where the wise men read his future.

carryVoice: Your line: a name is a wish. Tomorrow, a boy sits alone under a tree. Rest well.
